title: Godrej Properties' profit falls 62%, yet it lines up ₹32,000 crore of new homes
subtitle: The builder booked ₹8,008 crore of homes in July to September 2026. Here is why its profit still dropped, and what its big launch plan means.
content_html:
Picture this. A company sells homes worth ₹8,008 crore in just three months. Yet the profit it reports for those same three months is only ₹154 crore. Strange? Not for a builder.

That company is Godrej Properties. On Friday, 23 October 2026, it shared its results for July to September 2026. Its net profit fell 62% to ₹154 crore, from ₹405 crore a year earlier. But on the same day, its chief said the company has new housing projects worth more than ₹32,000 crore lined up for launch between October 2026 and March 2027.

So which is it: a bad quarter or a big plan? The answer is a little of both, and it shows how a home builder really makes money.

First, who is Godrej Properties?

Godrej Properties is the real estate arm of the Godrej Industries Group. It builds flats and offices. Mint calls it India's top-selling residential developer. Residential simply means homes where people live, not offices or shops.

Companies split their money year into four parts of three months each, called quarters. India's money year runs from April to March. So July to September 2026 is the second quarter, or Q2, of the year that ends in March 2027. People write that year as FY27.

Big sales, small profit: how?

Here is the key idea. When you buy a flat that is still being built, you sign up for it and start paying in parts. The builder calls this a booking. It is a bit like paying an advance for a cricket bat that the shop will make for you over the next few months.

The shop has your money, but it cannot honestly call the sale finished until you hold the bat. Builders work the same way. They count the profit only when the finished flat is handed over to the buyer. Godrej Properties' chairperson, Pirojsha Godrej, called this "project completion accounting". He said FY28 is the year when the strong growth of the past few years will start to show in the reported numbers.

That is why a builder's profit can jump up and down like a cricket score between overs. It depends on how many buildings were finished and handed over in that quarter, not on how many flats were sold. A summary of the company's earnings call says the weak profit came from the timing of project deliveries and the accounting effect of exits from joint ventures. A joint venture is a project a company builds together with a partner, like two friends sharing one samosa stall. Mint also points to higher costs.

The numbers, in plain words

In the quarter, Godrej Properties booked homes worth ₹8,008 crore, 6% lower than a year ago. That covered 3,658 homes. This was its seventh quarter in a row with bookings above ₹7,000 crore.

Its total income, which is all the money it recorded as earned, grew 38% to ₹2,575 crore, from ₹1,867 crore. Its EBITDA fell 72% to ₹171 crore, from ₹614 crore. EBITDA is the money a business makes from its daily work before paying interest on loans, tax and the slow wear and tear of its things.

One number grew very fast: sustenance sales. These are sales of homes in projects that were already on sale before, not new launches. They rose 83% to ₹5,054 crore. Four projects each brought in more than ₹500 crore: Godrej Trilogy in Mumbai, Godrej Vanantara in Bengaluru, Godrej Samaris in Gurugram and Godrej Brooklyn Avenue in Hyderabad.

How a builder earns, step by step

It helps to see the whole journey of one flat. A launch is the day a new project opens for sale, like a new cafe opening its doors. Buyers then book flats. While the building rises, they pay in parts. The builder calls this money collections. Finally, the keys are handed over, and only then does the profit enter the books.

The cash is the happy part

Profit on paper fell, but real cash coming in rose. Collections grew 31% to ₹5,318 crore in the quarter, the highest ever for a second quarter. For April to September, collections were ₹9,666 crore, up 25%. That means about ₹4,348 crore came in during April to June.

Its operating cash flow also rose 33% to ₹1,584 crore. Think of it as the cash left in the stall's box after paying for the daily lemons, sugar and cups. Pirojsha Godrej said the company expects ₹15,000 crore of collections and ₹7,000 crore of operating cash flow from October 2026 to March 2027.

The ₹32,000 crore plan

Now the big plan. Managing Director and CEO Gaurav Pandey said the company has a launch pipeline of ₹32,000 crore for the second half of the year. A pipeline is the list of projects waiting in line, like batters padded up and waiting for their turn.

Why does this matter? In April to September, the company launched only about one third of the projects it planned for the year. Even so, it reached 43% of its full-year bookings goal. Its bookings for those six months were ₹16,659 crore, up 7%, its best first half ever.

The full-year target is ₹39,000 crore of sales. For October to March, it expects bookings of ₹22,500 crore to ₹25,000 crore. Add the lower figure to the first half's ₹16,659 crore and you get ₹39,159 crore, just above the target. "Our launch pipeline has never been stronger," Pirojsha Godrej said on the call.

Where the new homes are

The new launches include costlier projects in places such as Bandra in Mumbai and Sector 63A in Gurugram, plus projects in Thane, Vikhroli, Noida, Neopolis in Hyderabad and Pune. New phases of several older projects are also on the list. Two named launches are Bandra Bay and Godrej Virano.

On buying new land, Pirojsha Godrej said the company will take up new projects only if they meet its return targets. In simple words, a new plot must promise enough money back for the effort, like a stall owner opening a second stall only if it will earn well.

What to watch next

The next six months are the real test. The company has to launch the projects on time, get buyers to book them and keep the cash coming in. It also has a target to deliver 13.5 million square feet of finished space this year. Every finished building that is handed over turns old bookings into reported profit.

So the next time a builder's profit looks tiny, check its bookings and its cash too. In real estate, the sale and the profit can be years apart.
